config.userPrompt:
You are locating a PUBLIC DOMAIN source text for a children's story.

THE REQUEST: {{INPUT}}

Work out which traditional tale is being asked for, then write ONE web search query
that will land on a page containing its FULL TEXT.

PUBLIC DOMAIN ONLY. These tales and collections are free to use — published before 1929:
  - Grimm, Household Tales
  - Hans Christian Andersen, Fairy Tales
  - Aesop's Fables
  - Joseph Jacobs, English Fairy Tales / More English Fairy Tales / Celtic Fairy Tales
  - Andrew Lang's colour Fairy Books
  - Charles Perrault, Histoires ou contes du temps passe
  - Kipling's Just So Stories, Carroll's Alice

If the request is NOT one of these — a modern character, a film, a franchise, anything
still in copyright — reply with exactly:
NO PUBLIC DOMAIN SOURCE: <what was asked for>
and nothing else. Do not substitute a different story and do not write one yourself.

WRITING THE QUERY, which decides whether this works:
- Name the tale, its collection and its author, then the words "full text".
- NO search operators. No site:, no quotation marks, no minus signs. They narrow the
  search onto catalogue and licence pages, which contain everything ABOUT the story and
  none OF it.
- Never include the words "public domain" — that finds copyright notices, not tales.

GOOD: The Three Little Pigs Joseph Jacobs English Fairy Tales full text gutenberg
GOOD: The Tortoise and the Hare Aesop Fables Townsend translation full text
BAD:  site:gutenberg.org "The Three Little Pigs" "public domain"

Reply with ONLY the query.

Turn this source text into a screenplay for a short cartoon.

WHAT THIS IS. The source below is a public domain tale. You are adapting it, not
inventing one. If the source text is missing, unreadable, or is not the story that was
asked for, say so plainly in one line beginning "SOURCE PROBLEM:" and stop.

TELL THE VERSION THE AUDIENCE KNOWS. This is the single most important instruction here.

The source text is your evidence for the WORDS and the SHAPE, not a running order to follow
to the letter. Old collections often carry extra episodes that almost every retelling since
has dropped — Jacobs' Three Little Pigs wanders off to a turnip field, an apple tree and a
butter churn after the brick house. Those episodes are authentic AND nobody remembers them.
A viewer who knows the story and does not see the story they know will simply think it is
wrong, and they will be right about the only thing that matters.

So: keep the spine everyone knows, and CUT any episode the source has that a modern telling
of this tale would not include. For The Three Little Pigs the spine is exactly this and
nothing more:
    straw house  ->  huffed down
    stick house  ->  huffed down
    brick house  ->  holds
    the wolf tries the chimney instead, and that is the end of the wolf.
- The three attempts and the escalation. Three, not five.
- The repeated line, VERBATIM every time — "Little pig, little pig, let me come in" /
  "Not by the hair of my chinny chin chin" / "Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow
  your house in". That is the part children say along with it. Never reword it.
- Old-fashioned phrasing where it is the good part. Modernise only what would confuse.

SIMPLE. Aim for FIVE scenes, not twelve. One scene per house, one for the chimney, one to
open. Resist adding anything the spine does not need.

KEEP IT FOR CHILDREN — the way a children's picture book does, not by rewriting endings.
- The traditional comeuppance stays if the tale is famous for it: the wolf comes down the
  chimney, lands in the pot the pigs have boiling, and that is the end of the wolf. Say it
  in one line, the way the storybooks do, and cut straight to the pigs being safe. Do not
  linger, do not describe it, do not make it frightening.
- Nothing else is eaten, killed or injured, and no character is described as suffering.
  The pigs whose houses blow down simply run to the next brother, every time.
- No blood, no bodies, no cruelty, no fear-for-its-own-sake. Menace is comic — this wolf
  is a blowhard who has met a better builder.

FORMAT — a plain screenplay, exactly this shape and nothing else:

TITLE: <the story's real title>

EXT. OR INT. LOCATION - DAY
Action in the present tense, one or two sentences. What we SEE.

CHARACTER
The line they speak.

CHARACTER
The line they speak.

RULES THAT MATTER TO THE FILM
- EXACTLY FOUR OR FIVE scenes. Each is one place, and REUSE locations: the brick house
  serves the huffing AND the chimney ending, so those are one scene, not two. The film has
  to build every set it names, so every new location costs.
- The whole film is 60-90 seconds. If it runs longer you have added something the spine
  does not need — cut it.
- TWO to FOUR speaking characters. Name them in CAPS the same way every time.
- Between 14 and 20 spoken lines. Shorter is better; the repeated exchange carries it.
- Action goes in ACTION LINES, never inside a character's dialogue. A character must
  never narrate what is happening — if nobody would say it out loud, it is an action
  line.
- Every action line names who does what: "The wolf huffs and puffs.", not "He huffs."
- THE NARRATOR. Write one, and write the cue EXACTLY as `NARRATOR (V.O.)` every
  single time — the parenthetical is not decoration. It is what marks the part as
  a voice with no body. Written as a bare `NARRATOR` it becomes a character who is
  DRAWN and STAGED, standing in every scene lip-syncing the narration, which is
  worse than having no narrator at all.

  The narrator exists because this is dialogue on a screen, not a book. A reader
  gets "and the wolf, still hungry, thought of a trick" for free; a viewer gets
  nothing. So the narrator carries exactly what the dialogue cannot:
    * the opening — who these characters are and what they have set out to do
    * every jump in time or place ("the next morning, at the turnip field")
    * any MOTIVE the dialogue assumes but never states. If a character suddenly
      mentions turnips, the line before it must establish why.
  One to three sentences per scene. Never narrate what the audience can already
  see — if the pigs are on screen building houses, do not say they are building
  houses.

  NARRATION PLAYS OVER SOMETHING. The narrator has no body, so a scene whose only
  content is narration is an EMPTY STAGE with a voice over it — the audience
  opens the film and sees scenery and nobody. Never write such a scene. The
  narrator's opening belongs in the FIRST scene that has characters in it, and
  those characters must be doing or saying something in that same scene.

  Format it like any other cue, inside a scene that has a cast:

      EXT. MEADOW - DAY
      The three little pigs stand at the gate with their bundles.

      NARRATOR (V.O.)
      Once upon a time, three little pigs set out to seek their fortune.

      FIRST LITTLE PIG
      I shall build my house of straw.

- No "THE END".

SOURCE TEXT:
{{INPUT}}

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
YOU HAVE NOW READ THE SOURCE. BEFORE YOU WRITE, APPLY THIS.

The source is old and complete. Most of it is NOT in the story people know, and
your job is the story people know.

The spine, and nothing else:
    1. Three pigs set out. One builds of straw, one of sticks, one of bricks.
    2. Straw house  — "little pig, little pig, let me come in" — huffed down.
    3. Stick house  — same exchange — huffed down.
    4. Brick house  — same exchange — IT HOLDS. The wolf cannot blow it in.
    5. THE CHIMNEY. This is the climax and it must be SHOWN, not summarised. The
       wolf announces he will come down the chimney; the pigs put a pot of water
       on the fire beneath it; the wolf comes down and falls in. Then the pigs
       are safe. THE END.

       "One line, do not linger" applies to the LANDING only. It does not mean
       skipping the mechanism. A wolf who says "I'll try another way" and is then
       declared finished by a narrator is a film with no ending — the audience
       never learns what happened, and the pot they never saw cannot pay off.

       Write these four beats, in this order, as real staged lines:
           WOLF          — announces the chimney
           A PIG         — calls for the pot to go on the fire
           NARRATOR (V.O.)— the wolf comes down
           NARRATOR (V.O.)— and that was the end of the wolf
       Then one short line of the pigs being safe. Nothing after that.

CUT EVERYTHING ELSE, however authentic it is. In particular, if the source sends
the wolf and the pig to a TURNIP FIELD, an APPLE TREE, a FAIR, or a BUTTER CHURN
— cut all of it. Those episodes are genuinely in the old text and are in almost
no modern telling; a viewer who knows this story will not recognise them and will
simply think the film is wrong.

Four or five scenes. Fourteen to twenty spoken lines. The brick house serves both
the huffing and the chimney, so it is ONE location.

CHECK BEFORE YOU ANSWER — count these in your own draft:
  * the word "chimney" appears at least once in DIALOGUE
  * a pot / cauldron / kettle of water is put on before the wolf comes down
  * no turnips, no apples, no fair, no butter churn
  * no line is written twice
  * four or five scenes, fourteen to twenty spoken lines
If any check fails, fix it before answering.

Write the screenplay now.
